subject: Geography
sub_topic: Important plateaus — Deccan, Chota Nagpur, Malwa, Meghalaya

concepts.name: Deccan Plateau: Geological Origin and Structural Characteristics
key_dimensions: Formation from Gondwana supercontinent and its Precambrian crystalline basement
Role of Deccan Trap volcanism (Cretaceous-Eocene boundary) in shaping the plateau
Tectonic tilting — westward slope vs. eastward drainage paradox
Distinction between the Deccan Trap lava region and the broader Peninsular Plateau

concepts.name: Deccan Plateau: Drainage Pattern and River Systems
key_dimensions: Eastward drainage of major rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery) despite westward tilt — UPSC trap
West-flowing rivers of the plateau (Narmada, Tapi) and their rift valley origin
Antecedent vs. consequent rivers on the plateau
Watershed role of the Western Ghats as the water divide

concepts.name: Deccan Trap: Soil Formation and Agricultural Significance
key_dimensions: Formation of regur (black cotton soil) from basaltic lava weathering
Moisture-retaining property of regur and its suitability for cotton cultivation
Geographical extent of black soil — Maharashtra, parts of MP, Gujarat, AP
Comparison with laterite soils formed on non-trap areas of the plateau

concepts.name: Western Ghats vs. Eastern Ghats: Asymmetry and Plateau Edge Characteristics
key_dimensions: Western Ghats as a continuous escarpment vs. Eastern Ghats as discontinuous and lower
Rain shadow effect of Western Ghats on the Deccan Plateau (semi-arid interior)
Passes (ghats) through Western Ghats — Thal, Bhor, Pal, Bhorghat — strategic and economic importance
Eastern Ghats interrupted by rivers — Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery

concepts.name: Chota Nagpur Plateau: Geological and Structural Identity
key_dimensions: Part of the Peninsular Plateau — extension of the Gondwana landmass
Composed of Archaean gneisses, granites, and Gondwana sedimentary formations
Location within Jharkhand — boundary with Gangetic plains and significance
Distinction from Deccan Trap region — no volcanic origin, older crystalline rocks

concepts.name: Chota Nagpur Plateau: Mineral Wealth and Industrial Significance
key_dimensions: Concentration of coal (Jharia, Bokaro, Raniganj), iron ore, manganese, mica, bauxite
Damodar Valley — coal-bearing Gondwana sedimentary sequences
Basis for heavy industries — Jamshedpur, Bokaro, Durgapur in proximity
Mineral belt overlap with Chhattisgarh plateau and Odisha uplands — boundary confusion trap

concepts.name: Chota Nagpur Plateau: Drainage and River Characteristics
key_dimensions: Damodar River — 'Sorrow of Bengal', flows eastward into Hooghly
Subarnarekha, Brahmani, and Son rivers originating from the plateau
Waterfalls formed due to hard rock terrain — Hundru, Dassam falls
Plateau acting as a drainage divide between Ganga and Mahanadi basins

concepts.name: Malwa Plateau: Location, Extent, and Physical Features
key_dimensions: Location — north of Vindhyas and Satpura, covering Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan
Volcanic origin — part of the Deccan Trap lava flows, black soil dominance
Bounded by Aravalli in northwest, Vindhyas in south, Bundelkhand upland in east
Gentle northward slope — rivers drain into Ganga system (Chambal, Betwa, Ken)

concepts.name: Malwa Plateau: River Systems and Drainage Significance
key_dimensions: Chambal River — originates in Malwa, flows north then east into Yamuna; ravine land issue
Betwa and Ken rivers draining northward — Ken-Betwa interlinking project context
Malwa as a divide between Deccan drainage and Ganga drainage systems
Chambal ravines (badlands) — soil erosion problem and geography linkage

concepts.name: Vindhya-Satpura Range: Role as Barrier Between Malwa and Deccan
key_dimensions: Vindhyas as structural hill ranges (not fold mountains) separating North and South India
Satpura Range — block mountains formed by faulting, parallel to Narmada rift
Narmada-Son fault line separating the Vindhya-Satpura system from the Peninsular Plateau
Historical significance as a cultural and political barrier in Indian history — UPSC overlap

concepts.name: Meghalaya Plateau: Detachment from Peninsular India and Geological Significance
key_dimensions: Separated from main Peninsular Plateau by the Garo-Rajmahal gap (subsidence during Cretaceous)
Composed of Precambrian crystalline rocks — continuation of the Gondwana shield
Three hill ranges — Garo, Khasi, Jaintia Hills — each with distinct geography
UPSC trap: Meghalaya Plateau is a part of the Peninsular Plateau, not the Himalayan system

concepts.name: Meghalaya Plateau: Rainfall, Vegetation, and Climate Anomaly
key_dimensions: Mawsynram and Cherrapunji — among highest rainfall zones in the world; funneling effect of Khasi Hills
Despite heavy rainfall, water scarcity in dry season — porous terrain and steep slopes
Subtropical broadleaf forest and biodiversity hotspot characteristics
Contrast with rain shadow areas — semi-arid conditions in parts of Garo Hills

concepts.name: Peninsular Plateau as a Whole: Unity and Sub-divisions
key_dimensions: Central Highlands (north of Narmada) vs. Deccan Plateau (south of Narmada) — key division
Chota Nagpur, Meghalaya, Malwa as sub-units of the broader Peninsular Plateau
Plateau's age — one of the oldest and most stable land masses (Archaean origin)
Distinction between the plateau proper and the coastal plains on its margins

concepts.name: Deccan Plateau: Rain Shadow Effect and Semi-Arid Climate
key_dimensions: Western Ghats blocking Arabian Sea monsoon — interior plateau receives less than 700mm rainfall
Consequence: drought-prone districts of interior Maharashtra, Karnataka, AP
Contrast between windward (Kerala coast) and leeward (Deccan interior) sides
Impact on agriculture — dependence on irrigation, tanks, and groundwater

concepts.name: Plateau Soils: Comparative Analysis Across Major Plateaus
key_dimensions: Deccan Trap / Malwa — black cotton soil (regur); Chota Nagpur — red and laterite soils
Meghalaya — acidic, peaty soils with high rainfall leaching
Laterite soil formation on Deccan periphery (Karnataka, Kerala uplands) due to heavy leaching
UPSC trap: Laterite soils are not confined to Deccan — also found in Odisha, Assam, Kerala

concepts.name: Mineral Resources: Comparative Distribution Across Plateaus
key_dimensions: Chota Nagpur — coal, iron ore, mica, bauxite (sedimentary + metamorphic context)
Deccan Plateau — manganese (Maharashtra, Odisha), bauxite, limestone for cement
Meghalaya — coal (non-coking), limestone, uranium deposits in Khasi Hills
Malwa — limited major minerals; more significant for agricultural resources

concepts.name: Chota Nagpur and Chhattisgarh Plateau: Boundaries and Overlap
key_dimensions: Chhattisgarh (Mahanadi basin) as a distinct plateau unit — different from Chota Nagpur
Iron ore deposits of Bailadila (Chhattisgarh) vs. coal of Damodar Valley (Chota Nagpur)
UPSC trap: Confusing Chota Nagpur with the entire 'Jharkhand-Chhattisgarh-Odisha mineral belt'
Tribal belt continuity — Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha — socioeconomic and political context

concepts.name: Plateau Edges and Escarpments: Significance of Ghats and Scarps
key_dimensions: Western Ghats as a fault scarp (not fold mountains) — steep western face, gentle eastern slope
Eastern margin of Chota Nagpur — gradual merging with Gangetic plains (no sharp escarpment)
Malwa plateau edge — Vindhya scarp facing north is prominent; used historically as a defensive barrier
Waterfalls at plateau edges — energy potential and biodiversity (e.g., Jog Falls, Chitrakoot)

concepts.name: Narmada-Son Fault Line: Structural Divide and Tectonic Significance
key_dimensions: Narmada and Son rivers flowing in opposite directions along the same rift valley
Fault-guided rivers — rift valley origin, not erosional valleys
Serves as the structural boundary between the Peninsular Block and the extra-peninsular zone
UPSC trap: Narmada flows west (into Arabian Sea) while Son flows east (into Ganga) — same rift origin

concepts.name: Meghalaya Plateau: Tribal Culture, Biodiversity, and Environmental Issues
key_dimensions: Khasi, Garo, Jaintia tribes — matrilineal society and customary land rights
Sacred groves (Law Kyntang) as traditional biodiversity conservation mechanisms
Coal mining (rat-hole mining) and its environmental and legal issues — NGT rulings
UNESCO and biodiversity significance — overlap with Indo-Burma biodiversity hotspot
